newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn denies it planning Bundesbank restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Bonn denies it planning Bundesbank restructuring.

text.p: The German Finance Ministry, dismissing statements from a member of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said on Thursday that it had no plans to streamline the Bundesbank before European monetary union.
"We currently foresee no changes to the Bundesbank law," a ministry spokeswoman told Reuters.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, speaking after a central bank council meeting, also rejected the speculation, saying he was unaware of any plans to reorganise the central bank.

Speaking in the southern town of Aschau, he said monetary union would not affect the responsibilities of the central bank's regional branches. But, regardless of monetary union, the Bundesbank would cut its offices to 120 from 164.

The Finance Ministry and Bundesbank were responding to Bonn politicians who had said the government planned to amend changes to Bundesbank law currently under consideration to streamline the central bank's structure.

Friedrich Merz, a CDU financial expert, told the daily Bild newspaper that after the scheduled introduction of the single European currency in 1999 there would be no need for a large central bank council and large number of employees.
He said the government planned to change the Bundesbank law to reduce the number of council members and employees, cut the length of terms served and reduce pay.

"If monetary union comes in 1999, we won't need a 17-member central bank council and 16,000 Bundesbank employees any more," Merz told the newspaper. "New council members should therefore no longer be appointed for eight-year terms."
Merz told Reuters he expected there would be a broader discussion in Bonn about the future of the Bundesbank once parliamentary deputies returned from summer recess in September.

Another CDU member, Heinz Schemken, told Bild: "If the Bundesbank law is changed ... salaries should be cut. It is not right that the Bundesbank president should earn more than the the chancellor and that Bundesbank council members should earn more than government ministers in Bonn."
"Central bankers can also be independent when they earn less," Schemken added.

The Bundesbank jealously guards its independence and recently forced the government to back down over a plan to revalue its reserves, a move which might have helped Germany to qualify for monetary union.
The Bundesbank, which has 17 council members including eight directorate members, said itself in April that it planned to streamline its branch network.
Members of the directorate are nominated by the federal cabinet and, after consultation, are appointed for at least two years and normally eight years.
The Handelsblatt business newspaper published a similar report earlier this week but gave no sources for the information.

Juergen Stark, state secretary to the finance ministry, told a briefing on Tuesday that the government had no plans to make any changes to an amendment in the Bundesbank law which is currently going through parliament.
"There are no changes planned to this amendment, which is aimed at bringing the Bundesbank law into line with the requirements of the Maastricht Treaty," he told reporters.
But he avoided commenting on whether a further change in the law could be made at a later date.
